old: In West Africa the kingdom of Ghana is growing rich on trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt.
new: In West Africa the kingdom of Ghana may already be taking shape, though its great trans-Saharan gold trade is not recorded until the 700s.
source: UNESCO General History of Africa III (1988), ch. 18, p. 475 (Kumbi Saleh's gold trade 'begins not later than the eighth century'; al-Fazari's reference late 8th c.) — archive.org/details/general-history-of-africa-vol-3

old: The kingdom of Ghana prospers from gold and salt trade in West Africa.
new: In West Africa the kingdom of Ghana is probably emerging, though written records of its gold trade begin only in the 700s.
source: UNESCO General History of Africa III (1988), ch. 18, p. 475 — archive.org/details/general-history-of-africa-vol-3

old: in the Niger delta region
new: in south-eastern Nigeria, east of the lower Niger
source: UNESCO General History of Africa III (1988), ch. 18, p. 477 (Igbo-Ukwu lies c. 35 km from Onitsha on the Niger, not in the delta) — archive.org/details/general-history-of-africa-vol-3

old: whose king Hummay converted to Islam around 1085
new: whose Muslim king Hummay (c. 1075–1086) founded the Sayfawa dynasty
source: UNESCO General History of Africa III (1988), ch. 15 (D. Lange), pp. 459-60: Hummay came to power c. 1075 (r. c. 1075-86) and 'was not the first Muslim ruler of Kanem' — archive.org/details/general-history-of-africa-vol-3

old: The Omani Busaidi rulers controlled Zanzibar and the Swahili coast
new: The Omani Busaidi rulers held Zanzibar and claimed the Swahili coast, though their Mazrui governors in Mombasa acted almost independently
source: UNESCO General History of Africa VI (1989), ch. 9 (A. I. Salim), pp. 211-12 — archive.org/details/general_history_africa_vi

old: by Andrianampoinimerina from about 1787
new: by Andrianampoinimerina from about 1785
source: UNESCO General History of Africa VI (1989), ch. 16, p. 413 ('In about 1785 Ramboasalama ... proclaimed himself king under the name of Andrianampoinimerina')

old: and Oman ruled Zanzibar and the Swahili coast
new: and Oman held Zanzibar and Kilwa, while its Mazrui governors in Mombasa were virtually independent
source: UNESCO General History of Africa VI (1989), ch. 9, pp. 211-12 (c. 1800 Omani presence 'significantly evident in only three main centres: Mombasa, Zanzibar and Kilwa'; Mazrui autonomous)

old: Egypt and Cyprus
new: Egypt (Cyprus was held by his exiled brother Ptolemy IX)
source: Wikipedia: Ptolemy IX Soter II (ruled Cyprus 105-88 BC; Cyrenaica under Ptolemy Apion until 96 BC) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemy_IX_Soter_II

old: Meroë declined in the 4th century CE, and Aksum's armies finished it around 350.
new: Meroë declined in the 4th century CE and seems to have already collapsed when Aksum's armies raided the region around 350.
source: UNESCO General History of Africa II (1981), ch. 10 (Hakem/Leclant), p. 293: 'the Meroitic kingdom had already collapsed at the time of Ezana's campaign'
Turchin, Adams & Hall 2006 (1.25M km² for 350), via Wikipedia: List of largest empires

old: Under Kaleb, northern Ethiopia, Eritrea, parts of Nubia and Yemen across the Red Sea
new: c. 1.25M km² around 350 under Ezana (Turchin, Adams & Hall 2006): northern Ethiopia, Eritrea and parts of Nubia; in the 520s Kaleb also ruled Yemen across the Red Sea
source: Turchin, Adams & Hall 2006, via Wikipedia: List of largest empires

old: c. 4th century (oral tradition)
new: date unknown (tradition; Delafosse placed him in the late 8th century)
source: UNESCO General History of Africa III (1988), ch. 13 (B. Barry), p. 129 — archive.org/details/general-history-of-africa-vol-3
Taagepera 1997 (1.1M km² for 1380), via Wikipedia: List of largest empires

old: to beyond Timbuktu and Gao
new: to beyond Timbuktu and Gao; c. 1.1M km² (Taagepera 1997, for c. 1380)
source: Taagepera 1997, via Wikipedia: List of largest empires

old: Longest reign of any Muslim ruler
new: Longest reign of any caliph
source: Wikipedia: Al-Mustansir Billah ('the longest of all the caliphs'); a longer reign by a Muslim monarch (Hassanal Bolkiah of Brunei, since 1967) now exists — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mustansir_Billah

old: North Africa, Egypt, Sicily, the Levant and the Hejaz
new: North Africa, Egypt, Sicily, the Levant and the Hejaz; Taagepera (1997) and Turchin et al. (2006) give c. 4.1M km² for 969, counting nominal Saharan lands
source: Taagepera 1997; Turchin, Adams & Hall 2006, via Wikipedia: List of largest empires

old: From the Atlantic to Tripolitania, plus southern Spain
new: From the Atlantic to Tripolitania, plus southern Spain; c. 2.0–2.3M km² (Taagepera 1997; Turchin et al. 2006)
source: Taagepera 1997 (2.3M, 1150); Turchin et al. 2006 (2.0M, 1200), via Wikipedia: List of largest empires

old: Egypt, Syria, Palestine and the Hejaz
new: Egypt, Syria, Palestine and the Hejaz; c. 2.1M km² (Taagepera 1997)
source: Taagepera 1997, via Wikipedia: List of largest empires

old: Under Ptolemy III: Egypt, Cyrenaica, Cyprus, the southern Levant and Aegean outposts
new: Under Ptolemy III: Egypt, Cyrenaica, Cyprus, the southern Levant and Aegean outposts; c. 1.0M km² (Taagepera 1979, for c. 301 BCE)
source: Taagepera 1979, via Wikipedia: List of largest empires

old: western Sicily and the Balearics
new: western Sicily and the Balearics; Taagepera (1979) gives c. 0.3M km² for c. 220 BCE, when Barcid Spain had replaced the lost islands
source: Taagepera 1979, via Wikipedia: List of largest empires
Taagepera 1997 (0.8M km² for 1550), via Wikipedia: List of largest empires
Taagepera 1997, via Wikipedia: List of largest empires

old: Along the Niger from Senegal's borders to present-day Nigeria
new: Along the Niger from Senegal's borders to present-day Nigeria; c. 0.8M km² (Taagepera 1997, for c. 1550)
source: Taagepera 1997, via Wikipedia: List of largest empires

old: Victor at the Battle of the Three Kings
new: Proclaimed sultan on the field of the Battle of the Three Kings
source: UNESCO General History of Africa V (1992), ch. 8, pp. 208-9 (Sultan Abd al-Malik died during the battle; Ahmad 'proclaimed king after the victory')

old: Ahmad al-Mansur, victor over Portugal at the Battle of the Three Kings in 1578,
new: Ahmad al-Mansur, who took the throne when his brother Abd al-Malik died during the victory over Portugal at the Battle of the Three Kings in 1578,
source: UNESCO General History of Africa V (1992), ch. 8, pp. 208-9
UNESCO General History of Africa VI (1989), ch. 16, p. 413 ('In about 1785')

old: Around 1787 Andrianampoinimerina
new: Around 1785 Andrianampoinimerina
source: UNESCO General History of Africa VI (1989), ch. 16, p. 413
